question: Five cards numbered 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 lie face up in a row. Ben and Ann take turns to pick up one card, Ben first, until one card is left. Ann wins if its number is odd, and Ben wins if it is even. Who can make sure to win, and how?

options.B: Ben, by picking up an odd card each time
options.C: Ann, by picking up an even card each time she can
options.D: Ann, by picking up an odd card each time
options.E: Nobody can be sure: it is a matter of luck

hint: Four cards are picked up. Who picks up the last of them?
solution: Four cards are picked up: Ben picks up the first and the third, and Ann the second and the fourth. If Ann picks up an even card each time there is one, both even cards are gone by the end, whatever Ben does, and an odd card is left. So Ann wins.

A.text: Going first does not help Ben: Ann picks up the last card and so chooses which one is left.

B.text: Ben picks up two cards, but there are three odd ones, so one of them is left. Ann picks up the even cards, and the odd one stays.

D.text: Picking up odd cards helps Ben. Ann has to pick up the even ones, so that an odd card is left.

E.text: Nothing is left to chance: the cards lie face up, and both players choose every move.

question: Ann cuts a strip of 12 squares into two pieces along a line between squares. Then Ben takes the piece he likes better, and Ann gets the other one. What is the largest number of squares Ann can be sure to get?
hint: Whichever way Ann cuts, which piece will Ben take?
solution: Ben takes the longer piece, so Ann gets the shorter one. The shorter piece is longest when the two pieces are equal, 6 and 6. So Ann can be sure of 6 squares.

A.text: 7 is the longer piece of a cut into 7 and 5, but cutting first does not let Ann choose. Ben chooses, and he takes the 7.

B.text: 11 is what Ann gets if Ben takes the piece of 1, but Ben takes the longer piece. Ann can be sure only of the shorter one.

C.text: 12 is the whole strip, but Ann has to cut it into two pieces, and Ben takes one of them.

D.text: 5 is what Ann is sure of after cutting the strip into 7 and 5. Cutting it in the middle gives her 6 for sure.

question: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 are written on a board. Ann and Ben take turns, Ann first. A move rubs out two of the numbers and writes their sum instead. When only one number is left, Ann wins if it is even, and Ben wins if it is odd. Who wins?

options.C: Ann, if Ben ever adds two even numbers
options.D: Ann, since the six numbers add up to an even number
options.E: Ann, since she makes the last move

hint: What happens to the sum of all the numbers on the board after a move?
solution: A move rubs out two numbers and writes their sum, so the total of the numbers on the board stays the same. The one number left at the end is therefore 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21, which is odd, whatever the players do. So Ben wins.

A.text: Going first does not help Ann: the last number is 21 whatever anyone does.

C.text: No slip of Ben's helps Ann: whatever two numbers are added, the total on the board stays 21.

D.text: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21, an odd number: three of the six numbers are odd.

E.text: Ann does make the last of the five moves, but the winner is decided by the number left, not by who moves last.

question: There are 10 stones on a table. Ann and Ben take turns, and Ann goes first. On each turn a player takes 1 or 2 stones. The player who takes the last stone wins. Ben plays as well as he can. How many stones should Ann take on her first turn to be sure to win?

options.D: Any number, since she goes first
options.E: She cannot be sure to win

hint: Which pile would you hate to face on your turn: 1, 2 or 3 stones?
solution: A pile of 3 loses for the player whose turn it is: after 1 or 2 stones, the other player takes the rest. In the same way 6 and 9 lose. Ann takes 1 and leaves 9. Each time Ben takes some, she takes enough to make 3 in that round, so he faces 6, then 3, and she takes the last stone.

A.text: Taking 2 leaves 8. Ben then takes 2 and leaves 6, and now Ann is the one who loses.

C.text: A player may take only 1 or 2 stones, so 3 is not allowed.

D.text: Going first does not win on its own: after a bad first move, Ann loses.

E.text: This takes an even pile to be a losing one. Here the losing piles are 3, 6 and 9, and 10 is not one of them.

question: Kate and Leo count up to 22 together, and Kate starts. She says 1, 2 or 3. After that, each of them in turn adds 1, 2 or 3 to the last number said, and nobody may go past 22. Whoever says 22 wins. Leo plays as well as he can. What number should Kate say first?

options.E: Any of 1, 2 and 3, since she starts

hint: To say 22 yourself, which number would you like to have said on your turn before?
solution: If Kate says 18, Leo can only reach 19, 20 or 21, and then 22 is in her reach. So 18 is a number to say, and in the same way so are 14, 10, 6 and 2. Kate says 2, then after each of Leo's turns she adds enough to make 4 in that round.

A.text: 3 is the biggest first step, but it follows no plan: Leo adds 3 and says 6 himself.

B.text: Kate may start only with 1, 2 or 3, so she cannot say 4.

D.text: 1 would win a race to 21, where the numbers to say are 1, 5, 9 and so on. Here the goal is 22.

E.text: Starting does not win by itself: if Kate says 1 or 3, Leo says 6 and wins.

question: Zoe and Max share a box of 12 matches. Zoe starts, and they go one after the other, each time picking up 1, 2 or 3 matches. Picking up the last match wins. Both of them play perfectly. Who wins?

options.B: Zoe, if she picks up 1 first
options.E: Zoe, if she picks up 3 first

hint: Try a smaller box first: who wins with 4 matches? And with 5?
solution: A box of 4 loses for the player whose turn it is: whatever she picks up, the other player picks up the rest. So 8 and 12 lose too. Whatever Zoe picks up from 12, Max picks up enough to make 4 in that round. He leaves her 8, then 4, and picks up the last match himself.

A.text: Going first is no help here: whatever Zoe picks up, Max can leave her 8 matches.

B.text: After Zoe picks up 1, Max picks up 3 and leaves 8. Zoe wins only if Max slips.

C.text: Nothing is left to chance: both players see every match and choose every move.

E.text: After Zoe picks up 3, Max picks up 1 and hands her a box of 8, which loses.

question: Mia and Tom play with a stack of cards. They take turns to remove 1 or 3 cards, and Mia goes first. Whoever removes the last card wins, and both play as well as they can. The stack may start with 10, 11, 12, 13 or 14 cards. For how many of these starts can Mia be sure to win?
hint: Find out who wins when the stack has 1, 2, 3 or 4 cards. What do you notice?
solution: Both moves remove an odd number of cards, so every move turns an even stack into an odd one and back. A player facing an even stack always leaves an odd one, so she can never leave 0 cards, and 0 is even. So even stacks lose and odd stacks win, and among the starts only 11 and 13 are odd.

B.text: 3 counts 10, 12 and 14, the stacks Mia loses from, not the ones she wins from.

C.text: This uses the rule of a game where 1, 2 or 3 cards may go, in which only 12 loses. Here nobody may remove 2.

D.text: Going first is not enough: from 10 cards, whatever Mia removes, Tom hands her an even stack again.

E.text: Both 11 and 13 are wins for Mia, and one of them was missed.

question: Lily and Sam play with two jars of coins, one with 3 coins and one with 5. Lily moves first, and then they take it in turns. A move is to take one or more coins out of one jar. Taking the last coin wins the game. Sam makes no mistakes. Which opening move lets Lily win for sure?

options.D: Any move, since she goes first

hint: Suppose both jars hold the same number of coins and it is your turn. What can the other player do after each of your moves?
solution: Two equal jars lose for the player whose turn it is: whatever she takes from one jar, the other player takes the same from the other. He always has a reply, so he takes the last coin. Lily makes the jars equal by taking 2 from the jar of 5, which leaves 3 and 3.

A.text: Emptying a jar leaves Sam 5 coins in one jar, and he simply takes them all.

B.text: Taking 1 leaves 3 and 4. The jars are still one coin apart, and Sam evens them up himself.

C.text: Taking 2 from the smaller jar leaves 1 and 5, further apart than before. The 2 coins had to come from the bigger jar.

D.text: Going first does not win on its own: after most first moves, Sam can make the jars equal.

question: Eva and Dan share a bowl of 12 sweets. They eat in turn, Eva first, and each time a player eats 1 or 2 sweets. This time the one who eats the last sweet loses. Dan never makes a mistake. How many sweets must Eva eat at the start so that she wins whatever he does?

options.C: She cannot be sure: 12 divides by 3

hint: Which bowl would you like to hand Dan: 1 sweet, 2 sweets or 3 sweets?
solution: A bowl of 1 loses for the player whose turn it is, since she must eat the last sweet. A bowl of 4 loses too: after 1 or 2 sweets, the other player leaves 1. In the same way 7 and 10 lose. Eva eats 2 and leaves 10, and each round she makes the two turns add up to 3.

A.text: Eating 1 leaves 11, and Dan eats 1 to leave 10. Eva then faces the very bowl she wanted to give him.

C.text: That is the rule when the last sweet wins. Here the last sweet loses, so the bowls to leave are 1, 4, 7 and 10.

D.text: Eating 3 would leave 9, but nobody may eat more than 2 sweets at a time.

E.text: Starting does not decide it: if Eva eats 1, Dan leaves her 10 and she loses.

question: Nina has a bag of 15 marbles and plays a game with Oscar. They move in turn, starting with Nina, and each move removes 1, 3 or 4 marbles from the bag. Whoever empties the bag is the winner. If Oscar always makes his best move, how many marbles must Nina remove at the start to win for certain?
hint: Start from an empty bag and mark each small bag as a win or a loss for the player about to move.
solution: A bag loses for the player about to move when every move leaves a winning bag. Going up from 0, the losing bags are 0, 2, 7, 9 and 14. From 15 only removing 1 leaves one of them, 14. From then on Nina can always hand Oscar another losing bag, until she empties it.

A.text: Removing 4 leaves 11. Oscar removes 4 as well and leaves 7, a losing bag for Nina.

B.text: Removing 3 leaves 12, a losing pile in a game of 1, 2 or 3. Here Oscar removes 3 and leaves 9, which loses for Nina.

C.text: Nobody may remove 2 marbles in this game, only 1, 3 or 4.

E.text: This takes 15 to be a losing bag for Nina. It is the bag of 14 that loses, and she can hand it to Oscar.

question: Two rows of counters lie on a table, one of 2 and one of 4. Rosa and Jack take turns, and Rosa goes first. On each turn a player either takes any number of counters from one row, or takes the same number from both rows at once. At least one counter must be taken. Whoever takes the last counter wins. Jack plays as well as he can. Which first move lets Rosa be sure to win?

options.E: Any move, since she goes first

hint: Some positions can be cleared in a single turn. Look for a small position from which every move leads to one of those.
solution: Rows of 1 and 2 lose for the player to move. Every move from there leaves one row, two equal rows or 1 and 1, and each of those can be cleared in one turn. From 2 and 4, taking 3 from the row of 4 leaves 2 and 1. Whatever Jack does next, Rosa takes the rest.

B.text: That leaves two rows of 2, and Jack takes 2 from both rows at once.

C.text: That leaves a single row of 2, and Jack just takes both counters.

D.text: That leaves 1 and 3. Jack takes 1 from the row of 3 and hands Rosa 1 and 2.

E.text: Going first is not enough: every move but one lets Jack take the rest or reach 1 and 2.

question: The number 12 is written on a board. Ivy and Paul take turns, and Ivy goes first. On each turn a player picks a divisor of the number on the board that is smaller than that number, and takes it away from the number. The number 1 counts as a divisor. A player who cannot move loses. Paul plays as well as he can. How many of Ivy's possible first moves let her be sure to win?
hint: Who wins when the board shows 1? And 2, 3 or 4?
solution: Odd numbers lose for the player to move. An odd number has only odd divisors, so any move leaves an even number, and from 1 there is no move at all. From an even number, taking away 1 leaves an odd one. So Ivy must leave an odd number: 12 - 1 = 11 or 12 - 3 = 9. That is 2 moves.

A.text: Not every move works: after 12 - 2 = 10, Paul takes away 1 and leaves 9.

B.text: 3 counts the moves that leave an even number: 10, 8 and 6. Even numbers are the ones Paul wins from.

D.text: 1 is a divisor too, and 12 - 1 = 11 wins as well as 12 - 3 = 9.

E.text: 12 is a winning number, not a losing one: Ivy can leave Paul an odd number.

question: Ann, Ben and 8 other children stand in a circle, with 3 children between Ann and Ben on one side and 5 on the other. Ann and Ben take turns, Ann first. On each turn a player sends home one of the two children next to them. Whoever sends the other player home wins. Who wins if both play as well as they can?

options.A: Nobody can be sure: it is a matter of luck
options.C: Ann, by sending home the children on the side of 3 first
options.E: Ann, since 8 is an even number

hint: Whoever sends home the last child between them on one side ends up next to the other player. When does a player have to do it?
solution: A player who sends home the last child between them on one side stands next to the other player, who then sends them home. So both avoid it while they can, and the game goes on until there is one child on each side. From 3 and 5 down to 1 and 1, six children are sent home, by Ann, Ben, Ann, Ben, Ann and Ben. Then Ann has to send home a last child, so Ben wins.

A.text: Nothing is left to chance: both players see the circle and choose every move.

B.text: Going first does not help: six children are sent home before someone has to give way, and then it is Ann's turn.

C.text: Which side Ann takes children from does not matter. Ben answers each move, and Ann still has to move when one child is left on each side.

E.text: An even number of children works against the first player: after six moves, it is Ann who has to give way.

question: Two dragons sit on the corner squares A1 and D4 of a 4 by 4 board, with rows A to D and columns 1 to 4. They move in turn, the dragon on A1 first. A move takes a dragon one square up, down, left or right, and a dragon must move when it is its turn. A dragon that moves onto the other one's square wins. Which dragon wins if both play as well as they can?

options.B: The dragon from A1, since it moves first
options.C: Neither: they can run round the board for ever
options.D: The dragon from A1, if it heads straight for the other
options.E: The dragon from A1, since the two are 6 squares apart, an even number

hint: Colour the board like a chessboard. What colours are the two dragons' squares each time the dragon from A1 has to move?
solution: A1 and D4 are the same colour on a chessboard, and every move changes the colour of a dragon's square. So each time the dragon from A1 has to move, both dragons stand on squares of the same colour and are never side by side: it can never win. The dragon from D4 can: it keeps closing in, and the dragon from A1, which must move every turn on a board of only 16 squares, is driven into a corner and caught within 10 moves of the game.

B.text: Moving first does not help here: each time the dragon from A1 moves, the two stand on squares of the same colour, never side by side.

C.text: A dragon must move every turn, and the board has only 16 squares. The dragon from D4 can drive the other into a corner.

D.text: Heading for the other dragon only helps the dragon from D4. The dragon from A1 is never next to it on its own turn.

E.text: An even distance helps the second dragon: after every move of the first one, the distance is odd, and the second can close in.

question: Jack puts two dice on the table, each with any face he likes on top. Then Jill may turn either die, both or neither upside down. On a die, the top and bottom faces always add up to 7. Jill wins if the two top faces then add up to a number that divides by 4. Who wins if both play as well as they can?

options.A: Jack, if he puts a 1 and a 2 on top
options.D: It depends on the faces Jack puts on top
options.E: Jill, but only when the two faces add up to an even number

hint: What does turning both dice over do to the total? And turning just one?
solution: If the total s divides by 4, Jill leaves the dice as they are. Turning both dice changes s into 14 − s, so if s is even and does not divide by 4, then 14 − s does. If s is odd, the two faces differ by an odd number d, and turning one die or the other gives 7 − d or 7 + d, and one of these divides by 4. So Jill always wins.

A.text: Jill turns the 1 over: 6 + 2 = 8, which divides by 4.

B.text: Moving first does not decide it here: whatever faces Jack shows, Jill has a way to make the total divide by 4.

D.text: Every pair of faces has an answer: Jill turns nothing, one die or both. No case is left for Jack.

E.text: Odd totals can be put right too: a 1 and a 2 become 6 and 2, which make 8.
